direct_claims: This chart compares pig production systems on two dimensions: greenhouse gas emissions and animal welfare cost.
The title states the comparison is specifically for pig production.
The subtitle defines welfare cost as based on the quantity of years lived weighted by quality-of-life scores from detailed welfare assessments.
The subtitle also states that a positive welfare cost is bad because it means there is a cost to animal welfare, while a negative value indicates benefits to welfare.
The y-axis measures emissions per kilogram deadweight.
The note says the chart is based on 91 pig production systems across the United Kingdom and Brazil, and that each dot represents one system.
The legend indicates the systems are grouped into housing or production types including Outdoor, Slatted, Slatted + Straw yard, Solid floor, Straw yard, and Straw yard + outdoor.
In this chart, lower values on the emissions axis indicate less greenhouse gas emitted per kilogram of pig output.
Welfare cost is constructed so that values below zero are better for welfare and values above zero are worse for welfare.

Because the data comes from systems in the United Kingdom and Brazil, the chart may be especially relevant to debates about how geography, regulation, and production style affect sustainability comparisons.
The chart does not provide uncertainty intervals, sample sizes by production type, or exact welfare-score methodology beyond the short subtitle, which limits how confidently one can rank categories.
The absence of an underlying data table means exact numeric comparisons between individual systems cannot be verified from the provided materials alone.

Many systems cluster around emissions of roughly 2 to 5 kilograms per kilogram deadweight and welfare costs between about 0 and 0.4. — derived from estimated cluster location in the scatter plot.

Instead, the spread suggests overlap among production types and a trade-off that is variable rather than fixed. — derived from category distributions and scatter spread.
The category names in the legend imply that housing design is one of the main structural differences being compared. — derived from reading category labels.
This chart matters because it addresses whether climate goals and animal welfare goals in food production can be pursued together or may conflict in some systems. — derived from chart variables.

If some systems achieve both relatively low emissions and relatively low welfare cost, that would suggest opportunities to improve both outcomes at once rather than treating them as unavoidable trade-offs. — derived from scatter distribution.

One visible outlier has emissions above 12 kilograms per kilogram deadweight and a negative welfare cost, indicating a system with relatively better welfare by this metric but very high emissions. — derived from approximate extreme point.
Another group of relatively low-emission systems appears around 1.5 to 3 kilograms emissions with modestly positive welfare costs. — derived from estimated low-emission cluster.
